summary: A country on the equator in northwestern South America whose name is Spanish for “equator,” encompassing the Andes, the Amazon rainforest and the Galápagos Islands.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1534 the Spanish conquered Quito, which had belonged to the Inca Empire, and orders such as the Franciscans and Dominicans began missionary work at once; the indigenous Andean beliefs gradually merged with the worship of Catholic saints, and Quito became famous for its colonial-era religious art. In the 19th century President García Moreno made Catholicism a pillar of the state and in 1873 consecrated the country to the Sacred Heart of Jesus; only the Liberal Revolution led by Eloy Alfaro in 1895 separated church and state. Catholicism is still the majority, but its share falls year by year.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: From the 20th century American evangelical missions entered Ecuador, and the evangelical radio station HCJB, which began broadcasting from Quito in 1931, had a profound influence; in 1956 five American missionaries were killed by the Waorani in the Amazon region, an event that caused an international sensation. From the 1960s evangelicalism grew greatly among highland indigenous communities such as Chimborazo, partly as a reaction against the traditional Catholic hacienda system.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are found mainly in large cities such as Quito and Guayaquil, linked to the spread of higher education and the influence of global secular culture on younger generations, and have gradually increased since the 21st century.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: These include denominations introduced in the 20th century such as Jehovah’s Witnesses and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons), and the traditional beliefs still retained by Amazonian and Andean indigenous peoples; for example, the sun festival Inti Raymi, which honors the sun, is still held in the highlands.

religion.background: The Inca Empire conquered the Ecuadorian highlands in the late 15th century and brought sun worship; after the Spanish conquest of the 1530s, Catholicism replaced the state religion and blended with indigenous beliefs. After independence in the 19th century, conservatives and liberals fought bitterly over the status of the church; church and state were one under García Moreno, and the Liberal Revolution of 1895 established a secular state. In the 20th century American evangelical missions entered the highlands and the Amazon region, making Protestantism the second-largest religion, and in recent years the non-religious population has also grown in the cities.

language.official: The official language is Spanish; Kichwa and Shuar are official languages for intercultural relations.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: After the Spanish conquest of the 1530s, Spanish became the language of administration, the church and commerce, and the mixed-race mestizo population gradually became the majority. After independence in the 19th century Spanish was the only national language, and markedly different accents developed in coastal Guayaquil and highland Quito. Today government, education and the media all operate in Spanish.

ranking.name: Quechua (Kichwa)
ranking.description: Quechua reached Ecuador with the northward expansion of the Inca Empire in the late 15th century, and in the colonial period Spanish missionaries used it as a lingua franca for preaching to indigenous people, which spread it further in the highlands, where the local variety is called Kichwa. From the 1980s the indigenous movement promoted bilingual intercultural education, and the 2008 constitution recognized Kichwa and Shuar as official languages for intercultural relations. Speakers are concentrated in highland provinces such as Imbabura, Chimborazo and Cotopaxi, but young people switching to Spanish has lowered the proportion.

language.history: Before the Incas arrived, Ecuador had many local languages such as Cañari and Puruhá, which were later replaced by Quechua and disappeared. After Spanish colonization, Spanish became the mainstream, while Quechua continued in the countryside and among indigenous communities, absorbing a great deal of Spanish vocabulary. The Amazon region still has more than ten indigenous languages such as Shuar and Waorani. In the late 20th century indigenous organizations rose and pushed for official recognition of indigenous languages and bilingual education.

ranking.name: Encebollado (tuna and onion soup)
ranking.description: A fish soup stewed from albacore tuna, cassava, tomato and spices, to which plenty of vinegar-pickled red onions are added before serving, often accompanied by banana chips or popcorn.
ranking.history: Encebollado originated in Guayaquil and Manabí Province on Ecuador’s Pacific coast, where fishing is well developed and the port of Manta is an important center of tuna fishing and processing. The soup began as an inexpensive breakfast for fishermen and dock workers and was later thought to cure hangovers, and weekend-morning eateries always have long lines. Coastal residents often regard it as the national dish, and competitions across the country select the best encebollado.

ranking.name: Ecuadorian ceviche
ranking.description: Fresh shrimp or fish is marinated in lime and orange juice with tomato, red onion and cilantro, with a generous amount of liquid, and eaten with popcorn or fried plantain chips.
ranking.history: Coastal indigenous people were treating raw fish with fruit juice and chili long before the Spanish arrived, and the limes and onions introduced by the colonists gave the dish its form. The Ecuadorian version differs from that of neighboring Peru in that the shrimp are usually blanched first and a tomato-based sauce is added, with so much liquid that it can be drunk with a spoon. Ecuador is one of the world’s major exporters of white shrimp, and the abundant seafood makes this dish representative of weekends and beach holidays in the coastal region.

ranking.name: Llapingachos (potato patties)
ranking.description: Mashed potato stuffed with cheese is pan-fried into small golden rounds and served with peanut sauce, a fried egg, sausage, avocado and a green salad; it is a home-style dish of the highlands.
ranking.history: The potato is native to the Andes and has been the staple of highland indigenous people for thousands of years. Llapingachos originated around Ambato and Tungurahua in the central highlands, and the name comes from Kichwa, combining the native potato with the cheese, eggs and pork products introduced in the colonial period. It often appears in highland markets and at family lunches, showing the blending of indigenous and Spanish food.
ranking.imageCredit: young shanahan from Bratislava, Slovakia・CC BY 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Fanesca
ranking.description: A thick soup cooked from pumpkin, many kinds of beans and grains, with rehydrated salt cod and milk, garnished with hard-boiled eggs, fried dough and plantain.
ranking.history: Fanesca is made only during Holy Week before Easter and traditionally includes twelve kinds of beans and grains, symbolizing the twelve disciples of Jesus, while the salt cod represents the Christian rule of fasting from red meat during Lent. It combines the Andean native squash, corn and beans with the salted fish brought by Spanish colonization, a typical example of Catholicism blending local produce after its arrival. It is very labor-intensive to make, and families often work on it together and share it with relatives and friends; families in Quito especially value this tradition.
ranking.imageCredit: Agencia de Noticias ANDES・CC BY-SA 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Locro de papa (potato and cheese soup)
ranking.description: Potatoes are cooked until half-dissolved into a thick soup, mixed with cheese, milk and annatto oil, and served with slices of avocado, creamy and warming.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Kichwa “ruqru,” originally referring to the thick soup that Andean indigenous people stewed from potatoes, corn and squash. After the Spanish brought dairy cows, milk and cheese were added to the soup, forming today’s version. In the cold Andean highlands, this warming soup is the most common lunch soup in homes and schools, and it also represents the continuity of the “potato culture” of the Ecuadorian highlands.
